topics.title: Chapter 6 — Software and Package Management
topics.summary: A server is missing one utility. An administrator downloads a binary from an unfamiliar website, copies it over a packaged executable, and forgets the change. Months later, nobody can explain why the host behaves differently from its peers. Package management exists partly to prevent this loss of provenance.

blocks.text: A server is missing one utility. An administrator downloads a binary from an unfamiliar website, copies it over a packaged executable, and forgets the change. Months later, nobody can explain why the host behaves differently from its peers. Package management exists partly to prevent this loss of provenance.

A package is not only a compressed program. It participates in a system of ownership, dependencies, trusted sources, configuration, updates, and removal. This chapter shows how to use that system without treating a successful installation as the end of operational responsibility.

topics.title: 6.1 Linux Packages
topics.summary: A software package bundles files and metadata such as name, version, architecture, dependencies, and installation actions. Package metadata lets an administrator ask which software owns a file and what should change during an update.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.code:
# Debian/Ubuntu:
dpkg-query -W bash
# RHEL family, alternative:
# rpm -q bash
cards.answer: Use one applicable branch; package metadata is distinct from the running executable's behavior.

blocks.text: A software package bundles files and metadata such as name, version, architecture, dependencies, and installation actions. Package metadata lets an administrator ask which software owns a file and what should change during an update.

Packages may include service units, users, directories, and scripts run during installation or removal. Therefore installing a package is a privileged change, not simply unpacking bytes. Review the proposed transaction, especially when it includes removals or new services.

A package version can include distribution-specific release information. Compare the complete version and vendor advisory context rather than only the upstream number. Enterprise distributions can backport fixes, so an older-looking upstream version is not by itself proof that a known vulnerability remains unpatched.
Linux example — 6.1
Query an installed package using the host's family.

# Debian/Ubuntu:
dpkg-query -W bash
# RHEL family, alternative:
# rpm -q bash

topics.title: 6.2 Software Repositories
topics.summary: A repository is a managed source of packages and metadata. The package manager uses its metadata to discover versions and dependencies. Repository trust depends on configured signing keys, metadata verification, transport, and the publisher’s release process.

concepts.definition: A repository is a managed source of packages and metadata. The package manager uses its metadata to discover versions and dependencies. Repository trust depends on configured signing keys, metadata verification, transport, and the publisher’s release process.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.code:
# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt-cache policy
# RHEL family, alternative:
# dnf repolist
cards.answer: Enabled sources should belong to the intended release and trust policy.

blocks.text: A repository is a managed source of packages and metadata. The package manager uses its metadata to discover versions and dependencies. Repository trust depends on configured signing keys, metadata verification, transport, and the publisher’s release process.

Transport encryption and package signing solve different problems. HTTPS protects a connection to a server; signature verification helps establish the provenance of signed metadata or packages. Neither proves that the software is appropriate for your workload.

Keep enabled repositories intentional and documented. An extra repository can affect future dependency resolution even when you installed only one package from it today. Record its owner, purpose, signing-key source, supported releases, and removal plan.
Linux example — 6.2
Inspect package sources without refreshing them.

# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt-cache policy
# RHEL family, alternative:
# dnf repolist
blocks.code:

apt-cache policy
# RHEL family, alternative:
# dnf repolist
blocks.title: Original Linux example

topics.title: 6.3 RPM
topics.summary: RPM is a package format and lower-level package-management tool used in the RHEL and SUSE families. It can query installed packages, list owned files, and verify selected metadata.

blocks.text: RPM is a package format and lower-level package-management tool used in the RHEL and SUSE families. It can query installed packages, list owned files, and verify selected metadata.

rpm -q bash
rpm -ql bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
blocks.code:
rpm -q bash
rpm -ql bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: The first asks whether a package is installed, the second lists its files, and the third asks which package owns a path. These are different questions and often form the quickest route from an unfamiliar file to its documentation.

Use DNF or the distribution’s higher-level manager for ordinary dependency-resolving installation. Installing a lone RPM directly can leave dependency resolution to you. Never use dependency-bypassing options as a routine fix for a transaction the manager rejects.
Linux example — 6.3
On an RPM host, list a package's files.

rpm -ql bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash

topics.title: 6.4 DNF
topics.summary: DNF resolves dependencies and manages packages from configured repositories. Typical operations include search, information, installation, removal, updates, and transaction history.

concepts.definition: DNF resolves dependencies and manages packages from configured repositories. Typical operations include search, information, installation, removal, updates, and transaction history.

cards.answer: Repository metadata queries may contact configured repositories.

blocks.text: DNF resolves dependencies and manages packages from configured repositories. Typical operations include search, information, installation, removal, updates, and transaction history.

dnf info nginx
dnf list --installed nginx
sudo dnf install nginx
blocks.code:
dnf info nginx
dnf list --installed nginx
sudo dnf install nginx
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: Review the transaction before accepting it. For automated changes, an unattended confirmation flag is appropriate only after the package set, repositories, and acceptance criteria are controlled.

DNF transaction history helps reconstruct what changed, but history undo is not a universal rollback. Older packages may no longer be available, script effects may not be reversible, and application data may have changed format. A reliable rollback plan includes compatible packages, configuration, and data state. (R12)

On a DNF host, inspect package metadata.

dnf info bash
dnf list --installed bash

topics.title: 6.5 APT
topics.summary: APT manages DEB-based systems using repository metadata. apt update refreshes package lists; it does not upgrade installed software. apt upgrade applies eligible upgrades under its documented constraints, while more expansive operations can alter the package set more substantially.

blocks.code:

blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: apt policy helps identify installed and candidate versions and their sources. Use it before assuming that a package will come from a particular repository.

For scripts, prefer the documented scripting interfaces such as apt-get and apt-cache, and establish explicit error handling. Do not remove lock files to bypass an active package operation. Determine whether another package process is legitimately running and allow it to finish or recover it through a reviewed procedure. (R13)

On Debian/Ubuntu, inspect the selected package version.

apt-cache policy bash
apt-cache show bash

topics.title: 6.6 DEB Packages
topics.summary: DEB is the package format used by Debian and Ubuntu. dpkg manages local package state and supports queries similar in purpose to RPM’s queries.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.answer: Paths can vary on merged-/usr systems; query the actual resolved path if ownership differs.

blocks.text: DEB is the package format used by Debian and Ubuntu. dpkg manages local package state and supports queries similar in purpose to RPM’s queries.

dpkg -l bash
dpkg -L bash
dpkg -S /usr/bin/bash
blocks.code:
dpkg -l bash
dpkg -L bash
dpkg -S /usr/bin/bash
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: A merged filesystem layout or package database convention can affect which exact path is recorded. When a file-ownership query fails, inspect the resolved path and package listing before concluding that the file is unmanaged.

For a trusted local package with dependencies available in configured repositories, a higher-level command such as apt install ./package.deb is usually preferable to an isolated dpkg -i. The leading ./ distinguishes a local file. Trust and compatibility still require review before installation.

List files owned by a DEB package.

dpkg-query -L bash
dpkg-query -S /bin/bash
blocks.code:

dpkg-query -S /bin/bash
blocks.title: Original Linux example

topics.title: 6.7 Installing and Removing Software
topics.summary: Installation should begin with a requirement: which capability is missing, which supported package supplies it, and what services or dependencies will change? After installation, verify the package, configuration, service state, and useful application behavior.

concepts.definition: Installation should begin with a requirement: which capability is missing, which supported package supplies it, and what services or dependencies will change? After installation, verify the package, configuration, service state, and useful application behavior.

cards.question: Explain 6.7 Installing and Removing Software. What does the source establish?
cards.answer: Installation should begin with a requirement: which capability is missing, which supported package supplies it, and what services or dependencies will change? After installation, verify the package, configuration, service state, and useful application behavior.

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?
cards.code:
# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt-get -s install nginx
# RHEL family, alternative; answering no prevents the transaction:
# sudo dnf --assumeno install nginx
cards.answer: Review dependencies and removals before approving a real transaction.

blocks.text: Installation should begin with a requirement: which capability is missing, which supported package supplies it, and what services or dependencies will change? After installation, verify the package, configuration, service state, and useful application behavior.

Removal also needs review. A package manager may propose removing dependent packages, and configuration or data may remain according to the command and packaging policy. On Debian-family systems, removal and purge differ in treatment of package-managed configuration, but neither should be assumed to remove every application-created file.

Inspect the proposed transaction using the manager’s simulation or assume-no facility. Record the package list before and after. For a service, check listeners and residual credentials as well as package state. “Package absent” does not prove “all access and data removed.”
Linux example — 6.7
Preview an installation without applying it.

# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt-get -s install nginx
# RHEL family, alternative; answering no prevents the transaction:
# sudo dnf --assumeno install nginx

topics.title: 6.8 Searching for Packages
topics.summary: Use package search to find candidates, then inspect descriptions and ownership. Search terms are clues, not proof that a similarly named package supplies the desired executable.

concepts.definition: Use package search to find candidates, then inspect descriptions and ownership. Search terms are clues, not proof that a similarly named package supplies the desired executable.

cards.question: Explain 6.8 Searching for Packages. What does the source establish?

cards.question: What should you check after this section’s example?

blocks.text: Use package search to find candidates, then inspect descriptions and ownership. Search terms are clues, not proof that a similarly named package supplies the desired executable.

dnf search 'network diagnostic'
dnf provides '*/dig'
blocks.code:
dnf search 'network diagnostic'
dnf provides '*/dig'
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: On Debian-family systems, apt search searches package metadata; apt-file, when installed and updated, can search repository file contents. dpkg -S only searches installed-package ownership.

This distinction prevents a common dead end: asking the installed package database to identify a command that has not yet been installed. Choose the query matching the state you are investigating. After installation, use command -v and the package ownership query to confirm the actual executable.
Linux example — 6.8
Search package descriptions.

# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt-cache search '^nginx'
# RHEL family, alternative:
# dnf search nginx
blocks.code:

# RHEL family, alternative:
# dnf search nginx
blocks.title: Original Linux example

topics.title: 6.9 Updating Systems
topics.summary: An update changes a compatible package set and may require service restarts or a reboot. Installing a fixed library does not necessarily replace the copy already mapped into a long-running process. A new kernel package does not replace the running kernel until an appropriate reboot path activates it.

blocks.text: An update changes a compatible package set and may require service restarts or a reboot. Installing a fixed library does not necessarily replace the copy already mapped into a long-running process. A new kernel package does not replace the running kernel until an appropriate reboot path activates it.
Apply updates first in a representative test environment. Include startup, application behavior, data access, and recovery checks. A package transaction completing is only one acceptance condition.

Classify urgency by exposure, exploitability, available mitigations, and business impact—not merely by how many packages are listed. Security and operations teams should share a decision process for emergency updates. Delaying every update indefinitely creates risk; applying every change without validation creates a different risk.

blocks.text: RHEL-family repository definitions commonly live under /etc/yum.repos.d. Debian-family sources may use traditional .list files or deb822 .sources files. The exact layout depends on the release and image.

Prefer repository-scoped key configuration rather than broadly trusting a key for unrelated sources. On APT systems, follow current Signed-By guidance instead of treating the deprecated global-key workflow as the default. Validate repository identity and distribution codename before enabling it.

After a change, refresh metadata and inspect candidate sources. A typo in a release name can produce no packages; a wrong but valid release can produce an incompatible package set. Successful metadata download is not proof that the source matches the operating system.

blocks.text: Third-party repositories can supply needed software, but they expand your software-supply chain. Evaluate publisher identity, signing practices, release compatibility, package naming conflicts, and the scope of future upgrades they can influence.

Do not pipe an unfamiliar download directly into a root shell. Download through a trusted channel, inspect the artifact and instructions, verify the publisher’s integrity mechanism, and understand the changes before execution. A checksum copied from the same compromised location is not an independent trust anchor.

Where possible, isolate application-specific dependencies from the base operating system. A virtual environment, container, or internal package can reduce conflicts, but each still requires updates and provenance. Isolation changes the management boundary; it does not eliminate responsibility.

blocks.text: Building from source can provide a needed feature or educational insight. The cost is that you may now own compiler selection, dependency tracking, security updates, packaging, and removal. A successful make does not create an operating procedure.

Build as an ordinary user in a dedicated workspace. Prefer a documented release archive or commit with verified provenance. Run tests before installation, and avoid sudo make merely because a build failed on permissions.

Install through a distribution package when practical, or use an explicit prefix such as a versioned directory under /opt. A staging directory can help inspect what installation would write. Record the source version, build options, toolchain, dependencies, checksums, and uninstall path. Do not overwrite package-managed files silently.

blocks.text: A patch plan connects package changes to service outcomes. Record the affected systems, approved repositories, expected transaction, restart requirements, maintenance window, validation, and rollback. Confirm that the recovery mechanism has been tested before relying on it.

Use a small canary group before a broad rollout. Watch the service long enough to exercise scheduled work, connection pools, and representative traffic. A server that passes a one-minute smoke test may still fail its nightly job.

Rollback must account for data compatibility. Downgrading an application binary after it migrated a database can be unsafe. Define the rollback point before the migration and document when forward repair is safer than reversal. Preserve evidence from a failed patch before restoring the previous state.

Gather prepatch evidence.

date -Is
uname -r
systemctl --failed --no-pager
df -h / /boot

labs.title: Detect drift in an installed-file fixture
labs.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
printf 'approved config\n' > config
sha256sum config > manifest
sha256sum -c manifest > /dev/null
printf 'changed\n' >> config
if sha256sum -c manifest > /dev/null 2>&1; then exit 1; fi
printf 'original verified; drift detected\n'
